This
mind is complete in itself; it is not to be sought outside.

The Buddha taught and expounded the Dharma for forty-nine years, and of those years twenty-two were given to the prajñā scriptures. It may be said that the prajñā scriptures are the soul of the whole Dharma, that the Diamond Sutra is the essence of the prajñā scriptures, and that the Heart Sutra is in turn the essence of the Diamond Sutra. That is why, for a thousand years, the Heart Sutra has been known in every household and on every lip.
The Heart Sutra Explained and
the Diamond Sutra Explained
are companion volumes, so much of their content is not repeated here. Please read the Diamond Sutra Explained first; you will then grasp the Heart Sutra Explained with deeper insight.
What does the Heart Sutra teach? The Heart Sutra teaches:
all dharmas are empty
(illusory)
, nothing whatsoever, nothing to be obtained.

The whole sutra sets forth the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, the Four Noble Truths, the six perfections, and other dharmas, in order to summarize the essential meaning of prajñā: “all dharmas are empty, nothing whatsoever, nothing to be obtained.” This is a teaching on the true nature of all dharmas; it is the supreme truth. In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury, the Buddha says:
“What is called the true nature of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.”
In the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra
volume forty, the Buddha says:

“All dharmas are false and deceptive; where they cease, that is called the real, that is called the true nature, that is called the dharma realm, that is called ultimate wisdom, that is called the supreme truth, that is called supreme emptiness.”
In the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines
volume ten, the Buddha says:
“All dharmas are like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage.”

[The five aggregates] Form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. [The eighteen elements] The six sense faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), the six sense objects (form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental objects), and the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness) are together called the eighteen elements. [The supreme truth] The highest, most perfect, and ultimate truth.

In the Buddhadharma, that which has appearance but no substantial reality (like things in a dream) is called “empty,” that is, an illusory appearance. When the Buddha spoke the word “empty,” it was to break the deluded minds of worldly people who cling perversely to all dharmas as truly existing. In the Sutra of Holding to the World, the Buddha says:
“Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusions, without reality, without any root.”
Therefore the meaning of “empty” is: like an illusion, without reality.

When a thing exists, we call it “existing”; when a thing does not exist, we call it “nonexistent.” But apart from “existing” and “nonexistent” there is yet another case: the illusory. It is like things in a dream—appearance present, reality absent—and so the concept “empty” is used to describe it. The Vimalakīrti Sutra
chapter three, “The Disciples,” says:
“All dharmas are ultimately nothing whatsoever; this is the meaning of emptiness.”

In this sentence, “all dharmas” means that appearance is present, and “ultimately nothing whatsoever” means that reality is absent. This case of appearance present and reality absent (the illusory) is what is called “empty.”
“Your letter asking for instruction is most sincere. But you have not yet grasped the two words “empty” and “illusory”
(correctly)

, and so you are not without obstruction regarding mind and objects, which is why your practice is hard to carry out. Now I shall explain it plainly for you, and you will be perfectly clear with no further doubt.
What is called “empty” is not an emptiness of utter nothingness
(the “emptiness” spoken of in the Buddhadharma does not mean being empty and nothing at all)
. … What is called the illusory is not the illusory of weird transformations, but
“existing yet unreal”
is what is meant
(the “emptiness” spoken of in the Buddhadharma is “appearance present yet reality absent”)

. It is like a peep-show box at the market, which draws out a host of figures and scenes. Yet within that box there is originally nothing at all, and suddenly there is something; though it exists, it is not real. Since it is not real, it is originally nonexistent, and because it is originally nonexistent we speak of emptiness. Therefore it is said: a phantom man is not nonexistent as a phantom man, but the phantom man is not a real man. If a man is not real, is he not empty?
The Buddha spoke the word “empty” to break worldly people’s clinging to it as truly existing; it was not to say that all is utterly cut off and annihilated.

Fearing indeed that worldly people might fall into annihilationism, he then spoke the word “illusory” to dispel their view of annihilation. Thus all dharmas of body and mind are empty because they are illusory, and because they are empty they are called illusory.”
(from the Dream Wandering Collection
“Instruction to Zhou Ziyin”)

[Peep-show box] A wooden box contained painted slides on rollers; on top of the box was a row of small round openings (three or four of them), with magnifying lenses set in the openings. After paying, customers would put their eyes close to the openings and look in. The box owner would then slowly turn a handle at the side of the box, and picture after picture passed in succession before the viewer’s eyes. Usually the pictures told a story one after another.

blocks.text: 2. The Medicine for a Suffering Mind

inline.s: The Heart Sutra is known in every household and on every lip because it is the great Dharma for transcending the illusory, saving all from suffering and distress. When Master Xuanzang journeyed west to fetch the scriptures, he crossed alone the eight-hundred-li desert of yellow sand, where no bird flew above and no beast walked below, and where he constantly met demons and spirits of strange and monstrous shapes that circled before and behind him; yet “he had only to recite the Heart Sutra, and at the sound they vanished.” This shows that the Heart Sutra is not only exquisite in its principles but also wonderfully efficacious when received, upheld, read, and recited.
What sentient beings see, hear, feel, and know is nothing but the appearances projected by their own karmic power; as it is said,
the wind of objects blows across the sea of mind, and karmic forces combine to raise the waves of consciousness.

The root of suffering is the habitual reaction of liking and disliking, grasping and rejecting, that arises from clinging to karmic appearances; and so beings ceaselessly create karma and receive its retribution, revolving through birth and death. Cultivation means putting a stop to this habitual reaction and cutting off the root of suffering. The Heart Sutra tells us how to do this and why it should be done. Doing so, one can be freed from suffering: in this life, to pass through suffering and distress; at life’s end, to end birth and death; until one perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

Among idioms there is the story of “the bow’s shadow in the cup mistaken for a snake,” a true tale told by Ying Shao of the Han dynasty: My grandfather Ying Chen was magistrate of Ji County, and on the day of the summer solstice he feasted the registrar Du Xuan, who was in charge of documents, and offered him wine. At the time, a red bow hanging on the north wall was reflected in the cup, and its shape looked like a snake. Du Xuan was both frightened and revolted, but because it was bestowed by his superior he dared not decline, and so forced himself to drink it down. As soon as he returned home, his chest and belly ached sharply, he ate and drank far less, and his body swiftly grew weak; every manner of treatment proved useless. Later, Ying Chen happened to visit Du Xuan’s house on business, and seeing him gravely ill, asked the reason. Du Xuan had no choice but to tell the truth: he had fallen ill from swallowing the snake in the cup. When Ying Chen heard this, he went home and pondered it a hundred ways without understanding: how could there be a snake in a wine cup? Suddenly he caught sight of the bow hanging on the wall and understood. Thereupon he ordered his attendants to bring Du Xuan in a cart and again set out wine for him in the same place. When Du Xuan saw the snake in the cup once more, he was greatly alarmed. Ying Chen then told him: it is not a snake, but the shadow of the bow hanging on the wall. He then moved the wine cup to another position, and the bow’s shadow disappeared. Only then did Du Xuan suddenly awaken; his doubts dissolved and his deep-seated illness instantly healed. (See the Comprehensive Meaning of Customs and Manners by Ying Shao of the Han dynasty.)
The moral of this idiom is that people often suffer because of their own misperception. At the same time, the story also shows the tremendous effect the mind has upon the body.

In truth, every one of us lives in an illusory world without knowing it, driven by illusory desires—struggling, suffering, aging, falling ill, and dying; and then again being born, again struggling, again suffering, again aging, again falling ill, and again dying; and so the cycle goes on without end. The true meaning and mission of human life is to be freed from this vicious cycle. The Sutra of Divining the Good and Evil Karmic Retributions says:
“Because the mind arises, all dharmas arise; because the mind ceases, all dharmas cease.”

Since beginningless kalpas, this mind has taken the false as real, and so beings wander through birth and death, suffering without cease. Now, to leave the false and return to the real depends entirely on this mind as well. The one who tied the bell must be the one to untie it; the illness of the mind must be cured with the medicine of the mind, and the Heart Sutra is our medicine for a suffering mind.
From what should one cultivate? This is a great question of deep concern to practitioners. The Treatise on the Essential Gateway to Sudden Enlightenment says with wonderful clarity:
“Question: What dharma should one cultivate in order to attain liberation? Answer: Only the one gate of sudden enlightenment brings liberation.
(Question:)
What is sudden enlightenment? Answer:
Sudden means suddenly eliminating deluded thoughts; enlightenment means awakening to nothing to be obtained.
(The Heart Sutra says:

“Because there is nothing to be obtained, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñāpāramitā, has no obstruction in mind. Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear, and he departs far from inverted dreams and reaches ultimate nirvāṇa.”
“Question: From what should one cultivate? Answer: Cultivate from the root.
(Question:)
What does cultivating from the root mean? Answer: The mind is the root.
(Question:)

How do we know the mind is the root? Answer: The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says: “When the mind arises, all dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all dharmas cease.” The Vimalakīrti Sutra says: “One who wishes to attain a pure land should purify his mind; as his mind becomes pure, the Buddha-land becomes pure.” The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching says: “Simply concentrate the mind on one point, and there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.” A sutra says: “The sage seeks the mind and not the Buddha; the fool seeks the Buddha and not the mind. The wise tame the mind and not the body; the fool tames the body and not the mind.” The Sutra of Buddha Names says: “Offenses arise from the mind and cease again from the mind.”
Thus we know that all good and evil come from one’s own mind; therefore the mind is the root.
One who seeks liberation must first recognize the root; one who does not comprehend this principle wastes his efforts
(squanders toil and labor)

, and seeking it in outward appearances will never succeed. The Sutra of the Chan Gate says: “Seeking in outward appearances, though one pass through kalpas, one can never succeed; observing inwardly with awareness, in the space of a single thought one realizes bodhi.””
The Heart Sutra tells us how to cultivate from the mind:
by relying on prajñāpāramitā.
The sutra says:
“Because there is nothing to be obtained, the bodhisattva,
relying on prajñāpāramitā
, has no obstruction in mind. Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear, and he departs far from inverted dreams and reaches ultimate nirvāṇa.”

Question: Who spoke the words of the Heart Sutra?

Answer: They were spoken by Avalokiteśvara, that is, the Bodhisattva Guanshiyin (Perceiver of the World’s Sounds). At that time Śākyamuni Buddha was on Vulture Peak, surrounded by his disciples. Avalokiteśvara was deeply practicing the dharma of prajñāpāramitā and contemplated the five aggregates as all empty. Then Śāriputra came to ask him for instruction, and Avalokiteśvara gave the following teaching (that is, the short version of the Heart Sutra). When Śākyamuni Buddha rose from samādhi, he approved what Avalokiteśvara had said and rejoiced in praise of it.
This may be seen in another translation of the Heart Sutra, the Prajñāpāramitā Heart Sutra (Dunhuang Cave Library version), translated by Facheng of the Tang
dynasty). Its text runs as follows:
“Thus have I heard: at one time the Bhagavān
(“Bhagavān” is the common title of all Buddhas)
was dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa
(Vulture Peak)
in Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of monks
(great bhikṣus)

and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Then the World-Honored One entered the samādhi gate of the profound and luminous dharma. And at that time, while the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara was practicing the profound prajñāpāramitā, he observed and saw that the very nature of the five aggregates was entirely empty. Then the venerable Śāriputra
(Śāriputra)

, empowered by the Buddha, addressed the noble bodhisattva-mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: ‘If a good man wishes to cultivate the profound prajñāpāramitā, how should he study it?’ Having spoken these words, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara answered the venerable Śāriputra, saying: ‘If good men and good women wish to cultivate the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should thus observe that the very nature of the five aggregates is entirely empty. Form is emptiness, emptiness is form. Form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form. So too are feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness all empty.’ … Then the World-Honored One rose from that samādhi and told the noble bodhisattva-mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: ‘Excellent, excellent! Good man, it is so, it is so! As you have said, so should they cultivate the prajñāpāramitā. All Tathāgatas will also rejoice in it.’”
Question: What is the evidence that Avalokiteśvara is the Bodhisattva Guanshiyin (Perceiver of the World’s Sounds)?
Answer: Master Kumārajīva’s translation of the Heart Sutra, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Mahāvidyā Sutra, says:
The Bodhisattva Guanshiyin
, practicing the profound prajñāpāramitā, contemplated the five aggregates as empty and passed beyond all suffering and distress.”
This shows that Avalokiteśvara is the Bodhisattva Guanshiyin.

blocks.text: The Text of the Heart Sutra

inline.s: Prajñāpāramitā Heart Sutra
Translated by decree by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty
When Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva was practicing the profound prajñāpāramitā, he illuminated the five aggregates and saw that they were all empty, and thus passed beyond all suffering and distress.
Śāriputra! Form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form. Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Śāriputra! This is the empty mark of all dharmas: neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.

Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, or mental objects; no realm of eye, and so forth up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance, and no ending of ignorance, and so forth up to no aging and death, and no ending of aging and death; no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path; no wisdom, and no attainment.
Because there is nothing to be obtained, the bodhisattva
(bodhisattva)
, relying on prajñāpāramitā, has no obstruction in mind. Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear; he departs far from inverted dreams and reaches ultimate nirvāṇa.
All Buddhas of the three times, relying on prajñāpāramitā, attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore know that prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great luminous mantra, the supreme mantra, the unequaled mantra, which can remove all suffering, true and not false.
Therefore he proclaimed the prajñāpāramitā mantra. The mantra runs: Gate, gate, pāragate, pārasaṃgate, bodhi svāhā.

blocks.text: The Meaning of the Heart Sutra

inline.s: When Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva
(Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva)
was cultivating the profound wonder of wisdom beyond the illusory
(practicing the profound prajñāpāramitā)
, he realized that body
(form)
and mind
(feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness)
are all illusory appearances, and so he peacefully passed beyond all suffering and disaster.

[Prajñāpāramitā] Reaching the shore of nirvāṇa by means of prajñā (wondrous wisdom). The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “What is meant by pāramitā? It is a word of the Western lands; in Chinese it means ‘reaching the other shore,’ and its meaning is deliverance from arising and ceasing. When one clings to objects, arising and ceasing begin, like waves on water—this is called the near shore. When one is free of objects and without arising and ceasing, like water flowing through without cease—this is called the far shore, and so it is named pāramitā.” The Diamond Sutra says: “All that has marks is false and deceptive.” “To be free of all marks is to be named a Buddha.” Therefore “prajñāpāramitā” is explained as “wondrous wisdom beyond the illusory.”
Thereupon he said to Śāriputra:
Śāriputra! Body
(form)
is an illusory appearance, and mind
(feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness)
is likewise an illusory appearance.
Śāriputra! All these dharmas are illusory appearances
(this is the empty mark of all dharmas)
, and in reality nothing is born and nothing ceases; there is no defilement and no purity; no increase and no decrease.
Therefore, within the illusory
(within emptiness)
there is in reality
no body or mind
(no form, no feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness)
; no six sense faculties
(no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind)
, no six sense objects
(no form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, or mental objects)
, no six consciousnesses
(eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness)
, which is to say there are no eighteen elements
(no realm of eye, and so forth up to no realm of mind-consciousness)
; no dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination cultivated by the pratyekabuddhas
(no ignorance, and no ending of ignorance, and so forth up to no aging and death, and no ending of aging and death)
; no dharma of the Four Noble Truths cultivated by the śrāvakas
(no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path)
; no dharma of the six perfections cultivated by the bodhisattvas
(no wisdom; since prajñā heads the six perfections, wisdom stands for them all)
; all of this—body and mind, the six faculties, the six objects, the six consciousnesses, the twelve links, the Four Noble Truths, the six perfections, and so on—is nothing to be obtained
(and no attainment)
The eighteen elements
The six sense faculties, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses are together called the eighteen elements.
Because there is nothing to be obtained
because there is nothing to be obtained
, the bodhisattva relies on the wondrous wisdom beyond the illusory
(the bodhisattva relies on prajñāpāramitā)
, and therefore has no obstruction in mind. Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear, and so he departs far from all inverted dreams and straightway realizes Buddhahood
(ultimate nirvāṇa)
All Buddhas of the three times, by relying on the wondrous wisdom beyond the illusory
(prajñāpāramitā)
, perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood
(attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi)
Therefore know: the wondrous wisdom beyond the illusory
(prajñāpāramitā)
is the great spiritually powerful mantra, the great luminous mantra, the supreme mantra, the unequaled mantra, which can remove all suffering, true and not false.

Therefore he proclaimed the mantra of the wondrous wisdom beyond the illusory. The mantra runs: Beyond the illusory! Beyond the illusory! Beyond the illusory, reach the other shore. May all be beyond the illusory and swiftly realize nirvāṇa
(Gate, gate, pāragate, pārasaṃgate, bodhi svāhā)
[Prajñāpāramitā Heart Sutra]

In the title, “prajñāpāramitā heart” is the specific title, while “sutra” is the common title. A specific title is one that only this sutra bears. The last word of the title of every Buddhist sutra is “sutra,” which all titles share in common and which is therefore called the common title.
Prajñā

,” rendered into Chinese, means wisdom. But this wisdom is not the cleverness and talent of the world; it is the wondrous wisdom that penetrates the true nature of the universe and of human life: that all things are dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows. The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says:
Prajñā is foremost among all wisdoms, supreme, unequaled, without equal, with none surpassing it.”
“Pāramitā”

, in the older translation, was “pārami” (the final syllable “tā” was not rendered). It means reaching the other shore, that is, passing from the near shore of ordinary beings, through the severing of the two deaths, to reach the far shore and attain Buddhahood.

[The two deaths] Segmentary death and transformational death. Within the three realms, the death of an ordinary being’s physical body is called segmentary death; beyond the three realms, each transformation of a bodhisattva’s mental state is exactly one death, and is called transformational death. [The three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by beings who have the two desires of sex and food, and includes the six heavens of desire above, humans and animals in the middle, and hungry ghosts and hells below; the realm of form is the world inhabited by beings who are free of the two desires of sex and food but still possess a physical body, and includes the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas; the formless realm is the world inhabited by beings who no longer have a physical body but dwell with their consciousness in deep and subtle samādhi, and includes the four heavens of emptiness (the heaven of infinite space, the heaven of infinite consciousness, the heaven of nothing whatsoever, and the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception). These three realms are all the domain of ordinary beings’ cycle of birth and death.
“Prajñāpāramitā”
, as seen from the sutra text, is in this sutra
a method of cultivation
. For example:

“When Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva was practicing the profound prajñāpāramitā, he illuminated the five aggregates and saw that they were all empty, and thus passed beyond all suffering and distress.” “The bodhisattva
(bodhisattva)
, relying on prajñāpāramitā, has no obstruction in mind.” “All Buddhas of the three times, relying on prajñāpāramitā, attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“Prajñāpāramitā” means: reaching the shore of nirvāṇa by means of prajñā (wondrous wisdom). The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“What is meant by pāramitā? It is a word of the Western lands; in Chinese it means ‘reaching the other shore,’ and its meaning is deliverance from arising and ceasing. When one clings to objects, arising and ceasing begin, like waves on water—this is called the near shore. When one is free of objects and without arising and ceasing, like water flowing through without cease—this is called the far shore, and so it is named pāramitā.”
The Diamond Sutra says:
“To be free of all marks is to be named a Buddha.”

Therefore, as a method of cultivation, the meaning of “prajñāpāramitā” is “wondrous wisdom beyond the illusory, accomplishing Buddhahood” (the practice of transcending the illusory). The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Not giving rise to deceit and delusion, but employing one’s own true suchness nature, contemplating with wisdom
(prajñā)
, neither grasping nor rejecting any dharma—this is seeing the nature and accomplishing the Buddha way.”
Prajñāpāramitā Heart Sutra
,” its Sanskrit being
Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra
. Among these, the word “heart” (Sanskrit
hṛdaya
) means the physical heart, and carries the sense of essence, heart-essence, and so on (the “heart” of the thinking mind is
citta

in Sanskrit). Therefore “heart” here means essence, heart-essence. This sutra condenses the enormously voluminous six hundred fascicles of the prajñā scriptures into a concise sutra that expresses “all dharmas are empty” (only

characters), and is thus the essence and core of the entire prajñā system. “Sutra” means a path, a way. Therefore “Prajñāpāramitā Heart Sutra” means: the essential path of the wondrous wisdom beyond the illusory that accomplishes Buddhahood.

However, the “mind” in the sutra’s phrase “no obstruction in mind,” whereby “there is no fear, and he departs far from inverted dreams and reaches ultimate nirvāṇa,” is the single thought of our own present mind—that is, the mind spoken of in the Sutra of the Great Vehicle’s Contemplation of the Mind Ground of Original Birth:

“The mind is like flowing water that does not stay a moment; the mind is like a gust of wind passing over a land; it is also like a monkey playing in a tree, and like an illusion produced by an illusion; like a bird flying in the sky, unobstructed, and like people running about in an empty village. Thus the dharmas of the mind are originally nonexistent, yet ordinary beings, clinging in delusion, say they are not nonexistent; if one can observe the nature of the mind as empty, delusion and obstruction do not arise, and one is liberated.”
Therefore this single thought of the mind is the key to cultivation, and cultivation means cultivating the mind. The Avataṃsaka Sutra says:
“Supreme bodhi takes the mind as its root; if the mind is pure, all roots of goodness are brought to perfection, and supreme bodhi is accomplished as soon as one wishes it.”
The Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, Spoken by the Buddha, says:
“This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the Buddhas’ universal knowledge arises from the mind’s thought.”
The Sutra of the Great Vehicle’s Contemplation of the Mind Ground of Original Birth says:
“All Buddhas take the Dharma as their great teacher, and the bodhi way is realized by cultivating the mind.”
In this sutra,

“Because there is nothing to be obtained, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñāpāramitā, has no obstruction in mind. Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear, and he departs far from inverted dreams and reaches ultimate nirvāṇa.”

This is precisely teaching us how to cultivate the mind, to pass beyond all suffering and distress, and to straightway realize Buddhahood. That is why, for a thousand years, people in their practice have deeply felt that “the Heart Sutra is the path (the shortcut) of cultivating the mind,” and so they receive and uphold the Heart Sutra as “the path of the mind,” “the sutra of the mind.” And when “prajñāpāramitā heart” in the title is understood as the mind of the wondrous wisdom beyond the illusory that accomplishes Buddhahood, the meaning of the title “Prajñāpāramitā Heart Sutra” becomes: the mind-dharma of the wondrous wisdom beyond the illusory that accomplishes Buddhahood.
[Perfectly universal knowledge] One of the ten titles of the Buddha. The Buddha possesses all wisdom and knows all dharmas without exception; hence he is titled the Perfectly Universal Knower.
Question: What is the relation between the Duoxin Sutra and the Heart Sutra?
Answer: The full name of this sutra is the Prajñāpāramitā Heart Sutra, and it circulates in the world under the short name Heart Sutra. In Master Kumārajīva’s transliteration of the Sanskrit word
pa^ramita^

, the final syllable was not rendered, giving “pārami”; Master Xuanzang’s transliteration gives “pāramitā.” Some people therefore misunderstood, thinking that “pārami” and “tā” were two separate words, and even took “tā” to mean dhyāna, samādhi; and so they abbreviated the Prajñāpāramitā Heart Sutra as the Duoxin Sutra (for example, in chapter nineteen of Journey to the West, “At Cloud-Stack Cave Wukong Subdues Bajie; On Pagoda Mountain Xuanzang Receives the Heart Sutra,” the Prajñāpāramitā Heart Sutra is called the Duoxin Sutra). Such a way of naming it is wrong.
[Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty, by imperial decree]
Xuanzang, the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty, translated this sutra by imperial command.

[Tripitaka Master] “Tripitaka” refers to the canon of sutras, the canon of vinaya, and the canon of treatises. The canon of sutras is the scriptures spoken by the Buddha; the canon of vinaya is the precepts laid down by the Buddha; the canon of treatises is the treatises composed by the Buddha’s disciples. A “Tripitaka Master” is a bhiksu who has mastered all three canons—sutra, vinaya, and treatise. [Xuanzang] Great Master Xuanzang (602–664), a celebrated Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty, is honored together with Kumarajiva and Paramartha as one of China’s three great translators of Buddhism, and he was one of the founders of the Consciousness-Only school. [Translated by imperial decree] Great Master Xuanzang translated this sutra by command of Emperor Taizong of the Tang.

Great Master Xuanzang was born in the second year of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty. As a child he followed his second elder brother, Master Changjie, and lived at the Jingtu monastery in Luoyang, where he studied the Dharma. At eleven (in 613) he had already memorized the Lotus Sutra and the Vimalakirti Sutra. At thirteen (in 615), when the monastic ordination examination was held in Luoyang, his excellent performance won him exceptional selection despite his youth. Thereafter he listened to Master Jing lecture on the Nirvāṇa Sutra, studied the Mahayanasamgraha with Master Yan, ascended the seat to repeat the teaching, and analyzed it so thoroughly that he won the admiration of the assembly.

[Ordination by examination] In ancient times, the court established a system for ordaining monks, in order to control the number of monks and nuns and to guarantee their quality, and it was forbidden to leave the household life privately. It was stipulated that one who wished to leave the household life had first to pass an examination on the Buddhist scriptures before being permitted to receive the tonsure.

Later, Great Master Xuanzang traveled on to study in various places and quickly exhausted the doctrines of every school; his talent was praised on all sides and his fame filled the capital. The minister Xiao Yu presented a memorial requesting that he be made to reside at the Zhuangyan monastery. Because he felt deeply that the teachings he had heard during many years of seeking the Dharma in various regions were inconsistent with one another—especially the theories concerning dharma characteristics held by the then-popular Shelun school (later absorbed into the Faxiang school) and the Dilun school, which often contradicted each other—he longed to obtain the Yogacarabhumi Sastra, which comprehensively encompasses the teachings of the three vehicles, in order to merge and penetrate everything. He therefore resolved to journey to India in search of the Dharma.

Because he could not obtain the travel document (passport) issued by the Tang court, his wish was never fulfilled. In 627, at the age of twenty-five, Great Master Xuanzang resolutely set out from Chang’an on his own, braving the journey to India (today’s India). Under exceptionally perilous and harsh conditions, with indomitable heroic spirit he overcame layer upon layer of hardship and obstacle and finally reached India.

During the more than ten years he spent in India, Great Master Xuanzang studied with and consulted many eminent masters. Among the monasteries where he stayed was Nalanda monastery, the celebrated Buddhist center then at the height of its fame. There he studied the Yogacarabhumi Sastra and other sutras and treatises with the abbot, the master of Indian Buddhist learning, the scholar-monk Silabhadra. Silabhadra was a disciple of Dharmapala and a second-generation disciple of Bodhisattva Vasubandhu. In the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era, Great Master Xuanzang, on behalf of Master Silabhadra, lectured at Nalanda on the Mahayanasamgraha and the Vijnaptimatratasiddhi Sastra. Thereafter, Xuanzang also traveled on foot to survey the whole of the South Asian subcontinent.

Great Master Xuanzang not only was deeply accomplished in the Dharma but was also fluent in Sanskrit, so he took part in religious debate assemblies again and again and won them all, his renown rising day by day. At the invitation of King Harsha he presided over the great unimpeded debate assembly on the meaning of the Dharma at Kanauj, extolling the Mahayana teaching. Those who gathered included the kings of eighteen kingdoms, more than three thousand monks of both the Greater and Lesser Vehicles, over two thousand Brahmins and exponents of non-Buddhist doctrines, and more than a thousand monks of Nalanda. The Master served as the chief disputant and instructed the assembly. He further declared: “If among my words there is a single one that is unreasonable and that someone can refute, I beg that my head be cut off in atonement.” Eighteen days passed, and in the end no one dared to come forward to dispute, so he won without a battle. When the assembly dispersed, everyone rejoiced, exclaiming that they had never seen the like. Thus his name rose suddenly, and his authority shook all of India; by the Mahayana practitioners of his day he was hailed as Mahayanadeva (Heaven of the Great Vehicle), and by followers of the Lesser Vehicle as Mokshadeva (Heaven of Liberation), and King Harsha paid him homage as his teacher.

In 643, Great Master Xuanzang set out for home laden with honor, bringing back 657 Buddhist scriptures to the Central Land. In 645 he returned to Chang’an and was warmly received and consoled by Emperor Taizong. In 652, in the western courtyard of the Ci’en monastery within Chang’an, he built a five-story pagoda (the present-day Giant Wild Goose Pagoda) to store the scriptures and images he had brought back from India. In 1962 a memorial hall to Great Master Xuanzang was established within the monastery. The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda has become an architectural monument to Xuanzang’s westward quest for the Dharma and his translation of scriptures upon his return.

With the strong support of Emperor Taizong, Great Master Xuanzang established a scripture-translation institute (a national translation academy) in Chang’an, and the outstanding scholars who took part in the translation came from throughout the country and from the nations of East Asia. He spent more than ten years within Yuhua Palace translating many scriptures into Chinese. These Buddhist scriptures later spread from China to the Korean peninsula, Vietnam, and Japan.
By translating Buddhist texts and expounding the scriptures, Great Master Xuanzang founded the Chinese Faxiang Consciousness-Only school, and his doctrine deeply influenced many other schools.

The sutras and treatises the Master translated in his lifetime total seventy-four works, altogether 1,338 fascicles, including the six-hundred-fascicle Great Prajñā Paramita Sutra—the most of any translator in the Central Land. Chinese Buddhism, through Great Master Xuanzang’s westward quest for the Dharma, which traced the matter to its very source, attained the complete essence of the Buddha’s teaching, and from then on flourished in China.

The Master passed away on the fifth day of the second month of the first year of the Linde era (5 February 664), and was buried on White Deer Plain. Tens of thousands of mourners attended the funeral; the emperor (Emperor Gaozong of the Tang) grieved and wept bitterly, and did not hold court for three days.

Profound Meaning” refers to setting forth, before the annotation of the text, the deep and subtle principle that this sutra expounds; this is the outline of the whole sutra. It leads the reader to grasp the general whole first and only then to study the text, so that the main points stand out and all is easy to comprehend and grasp.
The central idea (profound meaning) of this sutra is:
to leave illusion and emerge from the dream.
In the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra
Chapter Forty, the Buddha said:
“All dharmas are all false and unreal.”

This means that all dharmas are illusory appearances, like the affairs of a dream. In fact, all sentient beings, sunk in the dream of ignorance, experience all kinds of suffering and hardship; therefore to leave illusion and emerge from the dream is the core of the Dharma, the true meaning of prajñā paramita, and the essential point of the Heart Sutra.
In the Sutra of Complete Enlightenment, the Buddha said:

“All sentient beings, from time without beginning, have been in manifold inverted states, like a deluded person who shifts his direction again and again, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of his own body and the shadow-images of the six sense objects as the mark of his own mind. Like one with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon: in the sky there are in truth no flowers, yet the sick one grasps them falsely. Because of this false grasping, he is not merely deluded about the nature of empty space, but is also confused as to where the real flowers arise. Because of this false existence, he revolves in birth and death, and this is called ignorance. This ignorance has no real substance, like a person in a dream who, while dreaming, is not without something, yet upon waking finds nothing at all obtained. Like all the flowers in the sky, it vanishes into empty space and cannot be said to have a definite place of extinction. Why? Because there is no place of arising. All sentient beings, within the unborn, falsely see birth and death; therefore they are said to revolve in birth and death.”
(For the annotations, see
The Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Complete Enlightenment
In the Surangama Sutra, the Buddha said:

“You should know that all sentient beings, from time without beginning, continue in birth and death, all because they do not know the ever-abiding true mind, that nature that is pure, bright, and clear
(all because they do not know the pure, bright, clear nature that abides in the true mind)
, and instead give rise to all manner of false thought
(and go on to employ false thought)
; this thought is not true, and so there is revolution.”
This sutra says:
“When the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara practiced the profound prajñā paramita, he illuminated and saw that all five aggregates are empty, and passed beyond all suffering and calamity.”
This is the bodhisattva’s direct realization that body and mind are illusory appearances, and so he awakened and emerged from suffering. Again:

“Because nothing is attained, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñā paramita, has no hindrance in mind. Without hindrance, there is no fear; far from inverted dream-thoughts, he reaches ultimate nirvāṇa.”
and
“All Buddhas of the three times, relying on prajñā paramita, attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”
All speak of leaving illusion and emerging from the dream.
In
The Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
, there is a detailed discussion of the dream of ignorance and of how one leaves illusion.
Note: The headings in the text below have been added by the annotator and do not belong to the sutra itself.

blocks.text: 1. The Five Aggregates Are All Empty

inline.s: [When the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara practiced the profound prajñā paramita, he illuminated and saw that all five aggregates are empty, and passed beyond all suffering and calamity.]

When the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, cultivating the profound Dharma gate of wonderful wisdom that leaves illusion and realizes Buddhahood, in the samādhi of wisdom light illuminated and saw that body and mind are both illusory, he therefore passed calmly through all suffering and calamity.

Practice” is the wonderful wisdom that leaves illusion. “Profound” refers to the depth and degree of the practice. “Illuminate” means to contemplate with the light of wisdom inherent in one’s own nature.

Suffering is everywhere. And suffering arises from craving, and craving arises from clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind as “self.” So long as there is clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind, there is necessarily suffering; the deeper the clinging, the greater the suffering. Therefore it is said:
“illuminates and sees that all five aggregates are empty, and passes beyond all suffering and calamity.”

All sentient beings are endowed with the nature of awareness, luminous, clear, empty, and still, in no way different from the Buddha. But because, from kalpas without beginning, they have never awakened, they falsely cling to body and mind (form, feeling, thinking, conditioning, consciousness) as self (the mark of self), and so give rise to feelings of love and aversion, grasping and rejecting. Then, following their feelings, they create karma; following their karma, they receive retribution, and through birth, aging, sickness, and death they revolve through long kalpas.

[Avalokiteshvara] “Isvara” means self-mastery—existing autonomously. Sentient beings, from kalpas without beginning, are pulled and turned by objective conditions and false thought, wandering through birth and death without self-mastery. Avalokiteshvara means to break through the illusion of objective conditions and false thought, to achieve not turning with thoughts, not being pulled along by conditions, a mind without hindrance, and autonomous existence. Someone asked the Elder Master Guangqin: “Where should one begin in seated meditation?” The old master answered: “Begin with Avalokiteshvara.” (See the essay “The Fruit-Monk Who Is Free Everywhere.”) [Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva] Another name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara. The Dharma has two levels: one is self-benefit—realizing the Buddha path; the other is benefiting others—delivering sentient beings. Avalokiteshvara is named after self-benefit, and Avalokiteshvara is named after benefiting others. Master Kumarajiva’s translation of the Heart Sutra, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Great Bright Mantra Sutra, says:
“The bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, when practicing the profound prajñā paramita, illuminated and saw that the five aggregates are empty, and passed beyond all suffering and calamity.”

[The five aggregates] Also called the “five aggregates.” The five aggregates are the aggregates of form, feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness—the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called “dharma of form”; the four aggregates of feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness belong to the mental and are called “dharmas of mind.” The aggregate of form is the body; the other four aggregates (feeling, thinking, conditioning, consciousness) are the mind. Master Yinguang said:

“The five aggregates are form, feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness. Form is the body received as the retribution of karma; feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are the illusory, deluded mind that arises upon contact with objects. Through these illusory dharmas of body and mind, in the realm of the six sense objects, one stirs up confusion and creates karma.”
(From the Essence of Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings.) The Nirvāṇa Sutra says:

“At the moment of death, one’s kin and kindred weep. The person is terrified and cannot contain himself. The good and evil of a whole life all appear before his eyes. After the warmth is exhausted, the five aggregates of the past are extinguished, and the intermediate being of the present arises. After entering the womb, the intermediate being of the present is extinguished, and the five aggregates of the future arise. It is like a lamp being lit and darkness vanishing, and the lamp being extinguished and darkness returning—continuing without interruption.”
The Buddha Vipasyin said:

“Borrowing the four great elements to make a body, the mind is originally unborn but arises because of objects. If the objects before one are absent, the mind too is absent; guilt and merit, like illusion, arise and likewise vanish.”

(From the Compendium of the Five Lamps.) [The four great elements] The elements of earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water wetness as its nature, fire warmth as its nature, and wind movement as its nature. All tangible matter in the world possesses these four natures of hardness, wetness, warmth, and movement, and so they are called “great.” [If the objects before one are absent, the mind too is absent; guilt and merit, like illusion, arise and likewise vanish] Without objects there is no mind; without mind, guilt and merit vanish. Guilt is evil karma, merit is good karma; both are causes of the turning of birth and death. [The intermediate being] The intermediate being, also called the “intermediate existence” or “bardo,” is a transformation body formed of subtle matter that sustains life after death and before rebirth; this transformation body is the intermediate being. During the first forty-nine days, this intermediate being undergoes birth and death every seven days, passing through seven rounds of birth and death, awaiting the arrangement of karmic conditions, and then goes to take rebirth.
[Illuminates and sees that all five aggregates are empty] means to illuminate and see that all five aggregates are illusory. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra
Chapter Eleven, “The Study of Illusion,” says:

“Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from illusion? Are feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness different from illusion? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One......Form is not different from illusion; illusion is not different from form; form is illusion, illusion is form. World-Honored One, feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are not different from illusion; illusion is not different from feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness; consciousness is illusion, illusion is consciousness......The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? Does illusion have defilement and purity? No, World-Honored One. Subhuti, what do you think? Does illusion have arising and ceasing? No, World-Honored One.”
Read this chapter carefully, and you will know that “emptiness” in the Heart Sutra means “illusion.”

The root of all sentient beings, from time without beginning, sinking in the sea of suffering and revolving through the six paths of samsara is the false clinging to body and mind as real. In the Sutra of Complete Enlightenment, the Buddha said:

“All sentient beings, from time without beginning, have been in manifold inverted states, like a deluded person who shifts his direction again and again, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of his own body and the shadow-images of the six sense objects as the mark of his own mind. Like one with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon: in the sky there are in truth no flowers, yet the sick one grasps them falsely. Because of this false grasping, he is not merely deluded about the nature of empty space, but is also confused as to where the real flowers arise. Because of this false existence, he revolves in birth and death, and this is called ignorance. This ignorance has no real substance, like a person in a dream who, while dreaming, is not without something, yet upon waking finds nothing at all obtained. Like all the flowers in the sky, it vanishes into empty space and cannot be said to have a definite place of extinction. Why? Because there is no place of arising. All sentient beings, within the unborn, falsely see birth and death; therefore they are said to revolve in birth and death.”

Sentient beings create karma, receive retribution, and revolve precisely because they falsely cling to these five aggregates of body and mind as self! In the contemplation of the emptiness of the very self, this is what one should first look upon.

[Shadow-images of the six sense objects] The various thoughts that the six sense faculties produce by conditioning on the six sense objects; because these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadow-images of the six sense objects—the illusory reflections of conditioning on the six sense objects.
The Surangama Sutra says:

“You should know that all sentient beings, from time without beginning, continue in birth and death, all because they do not know the ever-abiding true mind, that nature that is pure, bright, and clear, and instead give rise to all manner of false thought; this thought is not true, and so there is revolution.”

(Translation: You should know that all sentient beings, from time without beginning, continue in birth and death all because they do not know that which abides in their own pure, bright, luminous nature, and instead employ false thought, taking body and mind as self, and so pursue objects and create karma; this false thought is not true, and so there is the turning of birth and death.)

[Passes beyond all suffering and calamity] Because all suffering and calamity are feelings of body and mind; once one awakens and directly realizes that body and mind are illusory, one no longer undergoes them. The Buddha said:

“Sariputra! Because form is empty, there is no mark of vexation and destruction; because feeling is empty, there is no mark of feeling; because thinking is empty, there is no mark of knowing; because conditioning is empty, there is no mark of doing; because consciousness is empty, there is no mark of perceiving.”
(From the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra
Chapter Three, “Practice and Response.”) [Suffering and calamity] hardship and disaster.
If one clings to existence, then feelings arise and suffering arises; if one destroys existence, then feelings vanish and suffering is extinguished—passing beyond all suffering and calamity.
[Clinging to existence] Falsely clinging to body, mind, and the world as real existence.

In studying the Heart Sutra, one should first work on “not dwelling on objects and thus giving rise to mind,” and in daily life realize that all objects and conditions are illusory appearances—dreaming and experiencing within a dream. “As all things pass before the eyes, one distinguishes good and bad; in the end, none of it concerns one.” When the effort matures, the mind becomes settled, prajñā arises of itself, and afflictions and karmic obstructions diminish day by day. Sometimes, if one is disturbed beyond endurance by past dust and former affairs, at once gather the mind in and respectfully recite the Heart Sutra, and the marks of karma will vanish of themselves.
Master Hanshan said:

“This one Prajñā Sutra speaks solely of a single contemplation of emptiness, and so is the first gate of entry to the Great Vehicle and the wondrous method of bodhisattva practice. The Sanskrit word ‘prajñā’ is here rendered as wisdom. Therefore, in benefiting living beings
(benefiting sentient beings)

, the bodhisattva takes wisdom as foremost. As it is said, ‘without wisdom, expedient means bind; with wisdom, expedient means liberate.’ Yet this contemplation of emptiness, though contained within the eight Prajñā divisions, is in its essentials found only in the fourteen lines of the Heart Sutra, which already include
(include)

everything. The Heart Sutra, a single fascicle, in turn lies solely in the line ‘illuminates and sees that all five aggregates are empty,’ which already exhausts its meaning. And within this single line, if one begins to practice, it lies only in the one word ‘illuminate’—this is the simplest and most essential gateway.”
(From the Dream-Wandering Collection
The Rite of Transformation and Rebirth.)

[Expedient means] The means, methods, or language adopted to guide and teach sentient beings. “Expedient means” is spoken in contrast to “ultimate reality.” [Without wisdom, expedient means bind; with wisdom, expedient means liberate] Here expedient means refers to benefiting sentient beings through manifold skillful means. The meaning of “without wisdom, expedient means bind; with wisdom, expedient means liberate” is: abiding in illusion (without wisdom) to benefit sentient beings results in being bound; leaving illusion (with wisdom) to benefit sentient beings results in liberation and freedom. Therefore, the bodhisattva should benefit sentient beings with wisdom (“the bodhisattva, in benefiting living beings, takes wisdom as foremost”). Hence, in delivering sentient beings, the bodhisattva should say: I shall liberate immeasurable sentient beings to extinction, yet in truth there are no sentient beings who are liberated to extinction. (For details, see
The Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
[Liberating sentient beings to extinction] Liberating sentient beings to Buddhahood.
The Vimalakirti Sutra says:

“Without wisdom, expedient means bind; with wisdom, expedient means liberate......What is meant by ‘without wisdom, expedient means bind’? It is when a bodhisattva abides in the afflictions of greed, anger, and wrong views, and yet plants the roots of all virtue—this is called ‘without wisdom, expedient means bind.’ What is meant by ‘with wisdom, expedient means liberate’? It is when one, leaving the afflictions of greed, anger, and wrong views, plants the roots of all virtue and dedicates it to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi—this is called ‘with wisdom, expedient means liberate.’”

[Planting the roots of all virtue] Accumulating various merits by benefiting sentient beings. [The Rite of Transformation and Rebirth] The gradual rules of expedient means for delivering sentient beings.

blocks.text: 2. Form and Emptiness Are Not Two

inline.s: From here down to the end of the sutra, all is spoken by the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara.
[Sariputra! Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form; form is emptiness, emptiness is form. Feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so.]

The great being Avalokiteshvara said to Sariputra: Sariputra! He who wishes to study this profound prajñā paramita Dharma gate should contemplate that the five aggregates are all empty: form (body) is not different from illusion, illusion is not different from form, form is illusion, illusion is form; feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness (mind) are likewise so.
In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra, Chapter Eleven, “The Study of Illusion,”

“the Buddha told Subhuti: ......Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from illusion? Are feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness different from illusion? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One.”

[Sariputra] This is Sariputra, one of the Buddha’s ten great disciples, renowned as “foremost in wisdom.” “Sari” is the name of his mother, and “putra” is rendered into Chinese as “son.” Sariputra is a transliteration; in translating scriptures there is also a combined transliteration-and-meaning rendering that translates it as “Son of Sari.”

[He who wishes to study this profound prajñā paramita Dharma gate, should contemplate in this way] The Song-dynasty translation of the Heart Sutra, the Buddha-Spoken Sutra of the Prajñā Paramita of the Holy Mother of Buddhas, says:

“At that time, the bodhisattva mahasattva Avalokiteshvara was in the Buddha’s assembly. This bodhisattva mahasattva, having been able to practice the profound prajñā paramita, contemplated that the self-nature of the five aggregates is all empty. Then the venerable Sariputra, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, came forward and said to the bodhisattva mahasattva Avalokiteshvara: If good men and good women, desiring to study this profound prajñā paramita Dharma gate, should study it, how should they study? Then the bodhisattva mahasattva Avalokiteshvara said to the venerable Sariputra: You should now listen attentively; I will proclaim it for you. If good men and good women desire to study this profound prajñā paramita Dharma gate, they should contemplate the five aggregates: their self-nature is all empty.

What is meant by the self-nature of the five aggregates being empty? Namely, that form is emptiness, emptiness is form; form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form. Feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so.
[Contemplation] Observing dharmas, both worldly and ultimate, with wisdom, and clearly illuminating and seeing them.

[Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form; form is emptiness, emptiness is form] This means that the body of form is an illusory appearance, wholly identical with illusion (emptiness), because from the standpoint of essence all are nothing at all. The Buddha-Treasure Sutra says:
“The marks of all dharmas are all a single mark, namely the mark of no-mark.”
(Translation: The marks of all dharmas are all the same single mark, and this “mark” is: nothing.)

Generally speaking, “form” refers to all matter that has shape and occupies space, and this line of the sutra also applies to it—all matter that has shape and occupies space is an illusory appearance. But here the sutra is further clarifying “the five aggregates are all empty”; here “form” is the aggregate of form among the five aggregates, referring specifically to the body of form.

Question: “Form is not different from emptiness” is easy to understand, because the aggregate of form is illusory. But “emptiness is not different from form” is difficult to understand. Does it mean that all illusory appearances are the aggregate of form?

Answer: Form and emptiness are not different, and this is said from the standpoint of essence (ultimate reality). From the standpoint of the dream of ignorance, the aggregate of form is only a part of all marks, so all marks contain the aggregate of form but are not identical to it. But from the standpoint of the ultimate reality of all dharmas,
“the marks of all dharmas are all a single mark, namely the mark of no-mark.”
(The Buddha-Treasure Sutra.) Since they are all the single mark of being nothing at all, there is no question of one containing the other; rather, they are mutually identical (not two).
Question: How does one contemplate?

Answer: Prajñā contemplation has two stages: understanding the principle (the meaning of the Middle Way, neither existence nor non-existence) and putting it into practice (the illusory-leaving practice of the dual operation of compassion and emptiness). Understanding the principle is the understanding, and putting it into practice is the practice. If prajñā contemplation is to have real effect, understanding and practice must correspond: form understanding according to the principle, and initiate practice according to the understanding. Jiang Weinong’s Lectures on the Diamond Sutra says:
“In reading the sutras and hearing the Dharma, the point is to be deeply vigilant
(reverent caution)
, and to take what the Buddha said as a mirror, using it at all times and in all places to illuminate oneself
(to use it to check whether one’s body, speech, and mind accord with what the Buddha said; accord is awareness, discord is delusion)

. Without contemplating and illuminating, by what means does delusion recollect itself? This is what is meant by relying on the words to arouse contemplation. When contemplation has been practiced for a long time, then, grand and majestic
(the appearance of great splendor)

, the vigilant mind arises of itself—this is the beginning of awareness, the first opening of the right wisdom inherent in the principle-essence. Practicing thus without retreating or slackening, the work of contemplation deepens and matures day by day. Then what is called the beginning of awareness is first like a crescent moon, gradually more light and less darkness, until the orb of the moon is full and its radiance shines brightly, and the essence of the nature manifests. That is the beginning of awareness uniting with the original awareness, and with no longer any division between beginning and original. Know that what is called becoming a Buddha is nothing other than the complete illumination of the nature of awareness.”
The Elder Master Xuyun said:

“The Patriarch Bodhidharma said: ‘One who clearly understands the essential school of the Buddha-mind, and whose practice accords with his understanding, is called a patriarch.’ Practice according with understanding means, what you can say you can do.
Do not be turned by objects. It is like herding an ox: hold the rope firmly, and if the ox will not obey, give it a few lashes.
If you can always subdue your mind thus
, then in time, as the effort deepens, there will be news of reaching home.”
(From The Elder Xuyun’s Expedient Instructions.)
The Essentials of Mind Transmission says:

“This original pure mind is always of itself perfect, bright, and universally illuminating. People of the world do not awaken; they only take seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving as the mind, and are covered by seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, so they do not behold the bright essential substance. But just directly set down the mind, and the substance appears of itself, like the great orb of the sun rising into empty space, universally illuminating the ten directions with no further obstruction. Therefore the student of the Way only takes seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, and all activity and movement; empty out seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, and the path of mind is cut off with no place to enter, but recognize the original mind right at seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving. Yet the original mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, nor is it apart from them. Only do not form views upon seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, nor stir up thoughts upon them, nor seek the mind apart from them, nor grasp dharmas by abandoning them; not identical, not separate, neither abiding nor attached, free in all directions—nowhere is it not a place of practice.”

[Feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so] This means that the mind is an illusory appearance—mental phenomena (feeling, thinking, conditioning, consciousness) are not different from illusion (emptiness). “Feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so” is an abbreviated statement; stated in full it is: feeling is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from feeling, feeling is emptiness, emptiness is feeling; thinking is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from thinking, thinking is emptiness, emptiness is thinking; conditioning is not different from illusion, illusion is not different from conditioning, conditioning is illusion, illusion is conditioning; consciousness is not different from illusion, illusion is not different from consciousness, consciousness is illusion, illusion is consciousness.
This passage of the sutra further clarifies that body (form) and mind (feeling, thinking, conditioning, consciousness) are all illusory appearances.
The Smaller Prajñā Paramita Sutra
Volume One says:

“Illusion is not different from form; form is not different from illusion; illusion is form, form is illusion; illusion is not different from feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness; consciousness is not different from illusion; illusion is consciousness, consciousness is illusion.”
The Great Prajñā Paramita Sutra
Volume Forty-Two says:
“Form is not different from illusion; illusion is not different from form; form is illusion, illusion is form; feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so.”
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra
Chapter Eleven, “The Study of Illusion,” says:
“Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from illusion? Are feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness different from illusion? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One.”
From this we know that “emptiness” in the Heart Sutra is exactly “illusion.”

This passage of the sutra further clarifies the above-stated “illumines and sees that all five aggregates are empty.” “Form” is the mark of the body; everyone grasps it as self, and with a self there is “mine,” and so one sets oneself at the center and opposes oneself to other people, affairs, and things. This is the root of self-grasping, the hardest to break. Therefore, at the beginning of entering contemplation, one first contemplates that this body is a temporary combination of the four great elements, originally not existing, wholly empty in its very substance. If the self-nature is not imprisoned by this body, then birth and death, coming and going, are without any hindrance—this is called the breaking of the aggregate of form.

If the aggregate of form is broken, then the four aggregates of feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness can be gradually contemplated deeply; for example: feeling is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from feeling, feeling is emptiness, emptiness is feeling; and so on, breaking them one by one.

In the Sutra of Complete Enlightenment, the bodhisattva Universal Eye requested the Buddha, for this assembly of bodhisattvas and for all sentient beings of the last age, to preach the gradual stages of bodhisattva practice: how should they think? How should they dwell and uphold? Since sentient beings have not awakened, what expedient means can universally bring them to awakening? The World-Honored One revealed:

“Good man! Those newly-learning bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the last age, who seek the Tathagata’s pure and perfect enlightened mind, should maintain right mindfulness and be far from all illusions. First, relying on the Tathagata’s practice of samatha, firmly uphold the precepts, peacefully house the assembly, and sit in meditation
(silently sitting in stillness)

in a quiet room, always thinking thus: This body of mine is a combination of the four great elements—so-called hair, fine hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, and the defiled color all return to earth; saliva, mucus, pus, blood, humors, spittle, phlegm, tears, essence and vital energy, and the excrement and urine all return to water; warmth returns to fire; movement returns to wind. When the four great elements each separate, where is this present false body? Then one knows that this body ultimately has no substance; being a combination it is a mark, and really is like an illusion. Through the temporary union of the four conditions, the six faculties falsely arise; the six faculties and the four great elements, combining within and without, falsely produce a breath of conditions that accumulates within; seeming to have a conditioned mark, it is provisionally called the mind. Good man! This false mind, if there were no six sense objects, could not exist. When the four great elements are dissolved, no sense object is to be obtained; within them the conditioned objects each return to dispersion and extinction, and ultimately there is no conditioned mind to be seen. Good man! For those sentient beings, because the illusory body is extinguished, the illusory mind is also extinguished; because the illusory mind is extinguished, the illusory objects are also extinguished; because the illusory objects are extinguished, the extinction of illusion is also extinguished; because the extinction of illusion is extinguished, that which is not illusion is not extinguished. It is like polishing a mirror: when the dust is exhausted, brightness appears. Good man! Know that body and mind are both illusory defilement; when the mark of defilement is forever extinguished, the ten directions are pure.”
[Samatha] The Chinese rendering is “stopping,” meaning the stilling of all sundry thoughts.

Emptiness” in many sutras means illusion—like the affairs of a dream, having marks but no substance—yet it is often misunderstood as a void (nothingness), especially by the followers of the Two Vehicles. Ordinary beings cling to marks (clinging to existence); the followers of the Two Vehicles annihilate marks (clinging to nonexistence). Both are attached to marks and fall into the two extremes. This passage of the sutra breaks both the ordinary being’s clinging to marks and the Two Vehicles’ annihilation of marks, revealing the meaning of the Middle Way.

[Clinging to marks] Holding all marks to be real. [Annihilating marks] Negating marks altogether. [The Middle Way] Neither clinging to marks nor annihilating them, but using marks with wisdom without being used by marks: to leave illusion by means of illusion is self-awakening; to deliver beings by means of illusion is awakening others. Neither clinging nor annihilating, the dual operation of emptiness and compassion—this is the meaning of the Middle Way.
“Form is not different from emptiness ... feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so”

, and this breaks the ordinary being’s clinging to existence. Because ordinary beings falsely cling to body and mind as real, they make plans for a thousand autumns and a hundred years. Little do they know that this body and mind is false and unreal, borne along by birth, aging, sickness, and death, thought after thought without pause, until old age and death—as the saying goes, “Where are the generals and ministers of former days? A heap of wild grass has swallowed their barren graves.” The Diamond Sutra says:
“All marks are false and vain.”

Ordinary beings do not know that body and mind are illusory marks, and so he tells them plainly: “Form is not different from emptiness ... feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so”—body and mind are emptiness (illusory marks).
“Emptiness is not different from form ... feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so”

, and this breaks the followers of the Two Vehicles’ clinging to nonexistence—discarding marks and guarding emptiness, attached to nothingness. In this way they may end segmental birth and death and escape the six realms of rebirth, but the attachment to dharmas is not yet removed; there remains transformation birth and death, and it is not ultimate. Therefore he tells them: “Emptiness is not different from form ... feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so”—causing them to awaken to true emptiness and also to accord with wondrous existence, to understand the essence and reach its function, perfectly fused without obstruction.
Having understood
“form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form ... feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so”

, the Great Being Avalokiteshvara further feared that students would still take the five aggregates and the emptiness of the five aggregates as two different things, still holding dualistic views. So he immediately taught further:
“Form is emptiness, emptiness is form; feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so”
, and thereby one enters the gate of non-duality.
The Vimalakirti Sutra
Chapter Nine, “Entering the Gate of Non-Duality,” in explaining how to enter the gate of non-duality, says:

“Form and the emptiness of form are two. Form is emptiness; it is not that form is destroyed and then there is emptiness—the nature of form is itself empty. Likewise, feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness, and the emptiness of consciousness, are two. Consciousness is emptiness; it is not that consciousness is destroyed and then there is emptiness—the nature of consciousness is itself empty. One who penetrates and understands this enters the gate of non-duality.”

Explanation: ordinary people suppose that form and the emptiness of form are two; in fact form is the emptiness of form, and it is not that form must be destroyed before there is emptiness, because the nature of form is originally empty. Feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are the same: for example, ordinary people suppose that consciousness and the emptiness of consciousness are two; in fact consciousness is the emptiness of consciousness, and it is not that consciousness must be destroyed before there is emptiness, because the nature of consciousness is originally empty. One who realizes this principle no longer holds the oppositions of form and the emptiness of form, feeling and the emptiness of feeling, thinking and the emptiness of thinking, conditioning and the emptiness of conditioning, consciousness and the emptiness of consciousness, and so on—this is entering the gate of non-duality.
Master Hanshan says in his Direct Explanation of the Prajñā Paramita Heart Sutra:

“If one contemplates in this way and knows that form is not different from emptiness, then there are no sounds, forms, goods, or profits to covet, and no five desires or dust-borne toils to long for: this is at once to cross beyond the suffering of ordinary beings. If one knows that emptiness is not different from form, then without rising from the samādhi of cessation one manifests all deportments; without moving from the original ground one performs the work of delivering beings. Dwelling in emptiness, the ten thousand practices seethe with activity; entering existence, the single path remains pure: this is at once to transcend the attachments of the non-Buddhists and the Two Vehicles.

“If one knows that form and emptiness are equal and one thus, then thought after thought one delivers beings yet sees no being to be delivered; mind after mind one seeks the Buddha yet sees no Buddha-fruit to be sought. This is what is meant by perfectly accomplishing the one mind, with no wisdom and no attainment; this is to transcend the bodhisattva [stages] and at once ascend to the other shore, the ground of Buddhahood.

“If one can contemplate the single dharma of the aggregate of form in this way, then the other four aggregates will in a single thought be perfect and bright. As it is said, ‘When one faculty returns to the source, the six faculties are all liberated.’ Hence it is said, ‘Feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so.’ If one can truly be thus, then all suffering is at once cut off and the Buddha-fruit may be reached. The other shore is not far; it lies only in this very person’s single thought of contemplating the mind brought to accomplishment. Is such a dharma not most profound!”

[The samādhi of cessation] Short for the samādhi of complete cessation. [Samādhi of complete cessation] Also called the samādhi of the cessation of feeling and thinking. In this samādhi the two mental factors of feeling and thinking are chiefly extinguished, and in the end even the mental factors of the six consciousnesses are extinguished; it is the last of the nine successive samādhis. Attaining this samādhi, one ends segmental birth and death and leaves the three realms. [Mental factors] Short for dharmas belonging to the mind—the various psychological phenomena that belong to the mind. [The nine successive samādhis] The successive samādhi of the first dhyana, of the second dhyana, of the third dhyana, of the fourth dhyana, of the sphere of infinite space, of the sphere of infinite consciousness, of the sphere of nothingness, of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the successive samādhi of the cessation of feeling and thinking. [The three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by beings who have the two desires of sexual union and food; from the six heavens of desire above down to the hells below, all belong to it. The realm of form is the world inhabited by beings free of the two desires of sexual union and food but still possessing form; the eighteen heavens of the four dhyanas all belong to it. The formless realm is the world inhabited by beings wholly without form who dwell with mind and consciousness in deep and wondrous samādhi; the four formless heavens belong to it. These three realms are all the sphere in which ordinary beings come and go in birth and death.

blocks.text: 3. The Empty Mark of All Dharmas

inline.s: [Empty mark] An illusory mark (a mark that appears illusorily).
[Sariputra! All dharmas are empty marks: neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.]
Sariputra!
All these dharmas are illusory marks (empty marks); in reality there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defilement nor purity, neither increase nor decrease.

[All dharmas are empty marks] All these dharmas are illusory marks (marks that appear illusorily). [Emptiness] In the Buddhadharma, that which has marks but no substance (like the affairs of a dream) is called “empty,” which is to say, an illusory mark. When the Buddha spoke the word “empty,” it was to break the world’s inverted thinking that falsely clings to all dharmas as truly existent. In the Sutra of Sustaining the World, the Buddha says:
“Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusions, without reality, with no root at all.”

In describing the existence of things, besides “existence” and “nonexistence” there is another case, that of illusory marks—like the affairs of a dream, having marks but no substance, not truly existing—and the concept “emptiness” is used to describe it. The Vimalakirti Sutra, Chapter Three, “The Disciples,” says:
“All dharmas are ultimately nothing at all; this is the meaning of emptiness.”

In this sentence, “all dharmas” means that marks exist, and “ultimately nothing at all” means that in reality there is nothing; this case of marks existing while in reality there is nothing (illusion) is called emptiness. Therefore “emptiness” and “illusion” are synonyms. Note, however, that in everyday usage “empty” means that there is nothing inside, as when we say: this room is empty.
[Neither arising nor ceasing] Originally there was never any arising, and so there is no ceasing either—there is nothing at all. The Vimalakirti Sutra
Chapter Nine, “Entering the Gate of Non-Duality,” says:
“Dharmas are originally unborn, and so now there is no ceasing.”
The Treatise on the Middle Way says:

“Neither arising nor ceasing, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither one nor different, neither coming nor going. He who teaches dependent origination, the wholesome stilling of all idle disputation—to that Buddha I bow in homage, foremost among all teachers.”
