These four lines, “neither arising nor ceasing,” reveal the foremost wondrous truth of true emptiness; no Buddhist sutra goes beyond this meaning. Originally there is not a single thing—how could there be any talk of arising and ceasing?

This passage teaches the reality of all dharmas: all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing at all. Therefore they are in reality “neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.”
[The reality of all dharmas] The actual situation of all dharmas. In the Buddha-Treasure Sutra
Chapter Two, “On Buddha-Recitation,” the Buddha says:
“What is called the reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing at all.”
In the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra
Volume Forty
the Kaundinya Chapter, the Buddha says: “All dharmas are false and unreal.” In the Sutra of Sustaining the World, the Buddha says:
“Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusions, without reality, with no root at all.”
(For a detailed discussion of the reality of all dharmas, see
The Reality of All Dharmas
In the prajñā scriptures, passages akin to this one abound. For example, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra
Chapter Two, “Receiving the Bowl,” says:
Because the real nature of all dharmas is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure,
the bodhisattva mahasattva practices thus, and likewise sees no arising, no ceasing, no defilement, no purity.”
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra
Chapter Eleven, “The Study of Illusion,” says:

“The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? Does an illusion have defilement or purity? No, World-Honored One. Subhuti, what do you think? Does an illusion have arising or ceasing? No, World-Honored One.”
In the Great Prajñā Paramita Sutra
Volume Two Hundred Ninety-Five, the Buddha says:
“Subhuti,
form is ultimately empty
, and therefore neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure;
feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are ultimately empty
and therefore neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure
, and thereby prajñā paramita is pure.”

When one has realized that “all dharmas are empty marks: neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing,” one can regard all things with equanimity, free of love and hatred, gain and loss, and no longer hindered. Dharmas are originally unborn—what joy is there in gaining? Dharmas are originally unceasing—what grief is there in losing? When the mind can be even, one is naturally without alarm, without dread, and without fear, and serenely enters the realm of freedom.

[Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, thinking, conditioning, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; no realm of eye, and so on up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, and so on up to no aging and death and no extinction of aging and death; no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path; no wisdom; nor any attainment.]

Therefore, within these myriad illusory appearances, there is in reality neither body, mind, objects, or conditions (worldly dharmas), nor the dharmas of the solitary realizer path, the hearer path, and the bodhisattva path (dharmas beyond the world); all are empty, utterly unattainable.
This passage of the sutra says: all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing at all, unattainable.
Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, thinking, conditioning, or consciousness;”
—that is, in illusory marks there is in reality neither body (form) nor mind (feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness)

[Therefore] The preceding line, “all dharmas are empty marks: neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing,” taught the reality of all dharmas—that the actual situation of all dharmas is nothing at all. From this the following conclusion is drawn: in ultimate reality there are no five aggregates, no eighteen realms, no twelvefold dependent origination, no Four Noble Truths, no six perfections and myriad practices; none of these is attainable. Hence the sentence begins with “therefore.” [In emptiness there is no form] In illusory marks there is in reality no form.
In the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra, the Buddha says:

“Good man! All sentient beings, from beginningless time, in all manner of inversion, are like a deluded man who mistakes the four quarters: deludedly taking the four elements as the mark of their own body, and the shadow-images of the six sense-objects as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in space and a second moon. Good man! In space there are truly no flowers; the sick person falsely clings to them. Because of this false clinging, he is not only confused about the nature of space itself, but also deluded about the place where the real flowers arise. From this false existence he revolves in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.”

This line of our sutra says that in reality there are no five aggregates, and the following text goes on to say that in reality there are no six faculties, six sense-objects, six consciousnesses, twelvefold dependent origination, Four Noble Truths, or six perfections. That is to say: the five aggregates are empty, the six faculties are empty, the six sense-objects are empty, the six consciousnesses are empty, the twelvefold dependent origination is empty, the Four Noble Truths are empty, and the six perfections are empty. This is what the Diamond Sutra says:
“All marks are false and vain.”

The emptiness of the five aggregates, the six faculties, the six sense-objects, and the six consciousnesses is the emptiness of ordinary beings’ dharmas, and so one leaves the dharmas of ordinary beings. The emptiness of the twelvefold dependent origination is the emptiness of the solitary realizer’s dharmas; the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths is the emptiness of the hearer’s dharmas; the emptiness of the six perfections is the emptiness of the bodhisattva’s dharmas; and so one leaves the dharmas of the sages. All are empty and all are left behind: “One who is free of all marks is called a Buddha.”
No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; no realm of eye, and so on up to no realm of mind-consciousness;”
in illusory marks there is in reality no
six faculties, six sense-objects, or even eighteen realms.

The five aggregates and eighteen realms (body, mind, objects, and conditions) are the hindrance of ordinary beings in the six realms; the absence of the five aggregates and eighteen realms breaks the ordinary being’s attachment to self.

[The six faculties] Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. [The six sense-objects] Form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas. [The six consciousnesses] Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. These are the discriminating functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, feeling, and thinking that arise when the six faculties meet the six sense-objects. [The eighteen realms] The collective name for the six faculties, the six sense-objects, and the six consciousnesses, namely: the realm of eye, realm of ear, realm of nose, realm of tongue, realm of body, realm of mind; realm of form, realm of sound, realm of smell, realm of taste, realm of touch, realm of dharmas; realm of eye-consciousness, realm of ear-consciousness, realm of nose-consciousness, realm of tongue-consciousness, realm of body-consciousness, realm of mind-consciousness. [No realm of eye, and so on up to no realm of mind-consciousness] “Realm of eye” is the first of the eighteen realms, and “realm of mind-consciousness” is the last of the eighteen realms. “No realm of eye, and so on up to no realm of mind-consciousness” is a summary statement that there are no eighteen realms.
No ignorance, and no extinction of ignorance, and so on up to no aging and death, and no extinction of aging and death;
in illusory marks there is in reality no dharma of the twelvefold dependent origination.
This breaks the solitary realizer’s attachment to dharmas.
“No ignorance, and no extinction of ignorance, and so on up to no aging and death, and no extinction of aging and death”
, meaning that the twelvefold dependent origination is also an illusory mark.

[The three times] Past, present, and future lives. [The twelvefold dependent origination] This explains the process by which sentient beings revolve in birth and death. The twelve links are: ignorance (the afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion, which are the root of birth and death), formations (the creating of all karma); consciousness (the karmic consciousness entering a womb), name-and-form (the fetal form, with the six faculties not yet complete), the six entrances (the fetus growing into a human form with the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), contact (birth as a human being and contact with objects), feeling (contact with objects giving rise to feelings of pleasure and pain), craving (desire and love toward objects), grasping (seeking and creating), becoming (forming karmic causes able to attract future retribution); birth (again receiving a future body of five aggregates), and aging-and-death (the future body gradually aging and dying). These twelve links take the delusion, karma, rebirth, aging, and death of the three times—past, present, and future—as their whole causal round, revolving again and again without end. Among them, ignorance and formations are karmic causes made in the past life; consciousness, name-and-form, the six entrances, contact, and feeling are retributions received in the present life; craving, grasping, and becoming are karmic causes made in the present life; and rebirth through aging-and-death is the retribution received in the future life (see the chart below). Contemplating the twelvefold dependent origination is the solitary realizer’s method of practice. [Solitary realizer] One who receives the Buddha’s teaching, contemplates the twelvefold dependent origination, awakens to the principle of true emptiness, and whose final fruit is the pratyekabuddha.
No suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path;”
in illusory marks there is in reality no dharma of the Four Noble Truths.

[The Four Noble Truths] The truth of suffering, the truth of accumulation, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path (abbreviated as suffering, accumulation, cessation, and path); “truth” here means reality. The truth of suffering sets forth the reality that life is full of suffering; in the truth of accumulation, “accumulation” means heaping up, and it sets forth the reality of how life’s suffering comes about; the truth of cessation sets forth the reality that only the state of nirvāṇa finally ends suffering; the truth of the path sets forth the reality of how one must cultivate the Way in order to realize nirvāṇa. These Four Noble Truths exhaust the two levels of cause and effect within and beyond the world: accumulation is the cause and suffering the fruit, which is the causal round of the deluded realm; the path is the cause and cessation the fruit, which is the causal round of the awakened realm. The Four Noble Truths are the hearer’s method of practice. [Hearer] One who hears the Buddha’s spoken teaching, cultivates and realizes true emptiness in reliance on the Four Noble Truths, and whose final fruit is the arhat.
No wisdom;”
in illusory marks there is in reality no dharma of the six perfections.
This breaks the bodhisattva’s attachment to dharmas.

[No wisdom] “Wisdom” here is prajñā wisdom, meaning that there are no six perfections and myriad practices of the bodhisattva. The bodhisattva’s six perfections and myriad practices are guided by prajñā (wisdom), and so one supposes that there is practice and there is wisdom, that there are beings to be delivered and a Buddha-fruit to be attained, and one cannot help clinging to the marks of this paramita practice. The Diamond Sutra says:
“The Buddha speaks of prajñā paramita, which is not prajñā paramita, and so it is called prajñā paramita.”

Therefore the most ultimate and perfect bodhisattva practice is the mutual fusion of compassion and emptiness: I should bring all sentient beings to extinction in nirvāṇa, and having brought all sentient beings to extinction, in truth not one being has attained extinction. The Diamond Sutra says:

“Thus I bring immeasurable, countless, boundless sentient beings to extinction, and yet in truth no being has attained extinction. Why? Subhuti! If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings, or the mark of a life span, he is not a bodhisattva.”

[Extinction] That is, nirvāṇa. “Extinction” means the extinction of the three kinds of delusion—the delusion of view and thought, the delusion numerous as dust and sand, and the delusion of ignorance; “crossing over” means crossing beyond the two kinds of birth and death—segmental and transformation.
Nor is anything attained.”
all the above (
the five aggregates and eighteen realms, the dharmas of the twelvefold dependent origination, the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths, and the dharmas of the six perfections
are nowhere to be attained.

Nor is anything attained” sums up what was said above: the five aggregates and eighteen realms, the dharmas of the twelvefold dependent origination, the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths, and the dharmas of the six perfections are all illusory appearances, all unattainable. For ordinary beings, not a single blade of grass or leaf of the body-mind world is attainable (much less glory, wealth, and the like); for the solitary realizers, neither the path of the solitary realizer nor its fruit (the pratyekabuddha) is attainable; for the hearers, neither the path of the hearer nor its fruit (the arhat) is attainable; for bodhisattvas, neither the bodhisattva path nor its fruit (Buddhahood) is attainable.
[No wisdom; nor any attainment] Another translation of the Heart Sutra, The Sutra of the Holy Mother Prajñā Paramita Spoken by the Buddha (translated by Dānapāla of the Song dynasty), says:

“Sariputra, therefore in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, thinking, conditioning, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; no realm of eye, no realm of eye-consciousness, and so on up to no realm of mind, no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance, no extinction of ignorance, and so on up to no aging and death, no extinction of aging and death; no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path; no wisdom;
nothing is attained, and there is no non-attainment either

From this we know that “nor is anything attained” sums up what was said above—the five aggregates and eighteen realms, the dharmas of the twelvefold dependent origination, the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths, and the dharmas of the six perfections—all of which are illusory appearances, all unattainable; and that it is not said merely of “no wisdom.” [Nothing is attained, and there is no non-attainment either] “Nothing is attained” is spoken with respect to essence; “no non-attainment either” is spoken with respect to mark. Therefore “attainment” is an illusory appearance that has mark but no substance.

In the Buddha-Treasure Sutra, Chapter Eight, “Pure Views,” the World-Honored One recounted in detail how in past lives he had attended and served many, many Buddhas, yet because he had something attained he did not receive the prediction, until the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha (also rendered as Fixed Light Buddha or Burning Lamp Buddha), when he awakened to the endurance of the non-arising—in the dharmas he in truth attained nothing—and so received the prediction:

“The Buddha told Sariputra: I recall that in past lives, seeking anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, I encountered thirty billion Buddhas, all named Śākyamuni, and in every case I was a wheel-turning sage king and made offerings throughout my life, and likewise provided clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for their disciples, seeking anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; yet those Buddhas did not give me the prediction, saying, ‘In a future life you shall become a Buddha.’ Why? Because I had something attained. Sariputra, I recall that in past lives I encountered eight thousand Buddhas, all named Dīpaṃkara, and in every case I was a wheel-turning sage king and made offerings throughout my life, and likewise provided clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for their disciples, seeking anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; yet none of those Buddhas gave me the prediction, saying, ‘In a future life you shall become a Buddha.’ Why? Because I had something attained. Sariputra, I recall that in past lives I encountered sixty thousand Buddhas, all named Light, and in every case I was a wheel-turning sage king and made offerings throughout my life, and likewise provided clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for their disciples, seeking anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; yet those Buddhas likewise did not give me the prediction, saying, ‘In a future life you shall become a Buddha.’ Why? Because I had something attained. Sariputra, I recall that in past lives I encountered three billion Buddhas, all named Puṣya, and at that time I was a wheel-turning sage king who made the four kinds of offerings; none of them gave me the prediction, because I had something attained. Sariputra, I recall that in past lives I encountered ... Thus in turn, until I met Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I attained the endurance of the non-arising; then he gave me the prediction, saying: In a future life, after asamkhya kalpas, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathagata, Worthy One, Rightly and Universally Knowing One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.”

[Receiving the prediction] Also written “bestowing the prediction”: the Buddha’s beforehand naming of a bodhisattva—after how many ages, in what place and what land, what Buddha he will become. [Endurance of the non-arising] Short for “the endurance of the non-arising of dharmas.” “Non-arising dharmas” refers to the principle-substance of true suchness, which is neither arising nor ceasing. When true wisdom abides securely on this principle and never again retreats or falls, it is called “the endurance of the non-arising of dharmas.”
In the Diamond Sutra,

“the Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? When the Tathagata was formerly with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did he obtain anything in the Dharma? No, World-Honored One! When the Tathagata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, in truth in the Dharma there was nothing obtained.”

[Dīpaṃkara Buddha] Also rendered as the Burning Lamp Buddha, the Universal Light Buddha, or the Fixed Light Buddha. [When the Tathagata was formerly with Dīpaṃkara Buddha] In the past, when the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva of the seventh ground, he met Dīpaṃkara Buddha and heard the Dharma, realized the endurance of the non-arising of dharmas, and ascended to the eighth ground; Dīpaṃkara Buddha then gave him the prediction, saying: After ninety-one kalpas, in an age called the Good Kalpa, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. [The Good Kalpa] The past great kalpa is called the Adornment Kalpa, the future great kalpa is called the Star Constellation Kalpa, and the Good Kalpa is the present great kalpa; because a thousand Buddhas appear in the world during this great kalpa, it is called the “Good Kalpa.”
In the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra, the Buddha says:
“All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in empty space.”
It also says:
“Birth and death and nirvāṇa, ordinary beings and all the Buddhas, are alike the marks of flowers in the sky.”
In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra, Chapter Three, “Practice in Accordance,” the Buddha says:
“There is no Buddha, and no Buddha-path either.”

The attachments of ordinary beings and sages alike have their root in the wish to attain something. But the truth of the matter is this: all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing at all, unattainable. Delusion is delusion over the mind of gain and loss—what is called being startled by gain and loss. When the mind of gain and loss comes to rest, that is great self-mastery.

The above has shown that the five aggregates and eighteen realms—the emptiness of self of ordinary beings—and the dharmas of the three vehicles beyond the world (the twelvefold dependent origination, the Four Noble Truths, and the six perfections) are empty, all unattainable.

The emptiness of the five aggregates and eighteen realms cuts off ordinary sentiment (breaking the attachment to self and severing the affliction obstruction); the emptiness of the dharmas of the three vehicles beyond the world removes sagely understanding (breaking the attachment to dharmas and severing the obstruction of the knowable).

[Attachment to self] Falsely clinging to body, mind, and world as truly existent. [Attachment to dharmas] Falsely clinging to the Buddhadharma as truly existent, supposing that there is a dharma to practice, a path to cultivate, and a fruit to attain. Where there is attachment to dharmas, there is transformation birth and death. [The two obstructions] The affliction obstruction and the obstruction of the knowable. First, the affliction obstruction, arising from attachment to self (the view of a person-self): with all the afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion it sets karma in motion and waters rebirth, vexing the body and mind of sentient beings, causing them to revolve in birth and death within the six realms and obstructing the fruit beyond the world. Second, the obstruction of the knowable, arising from attachment to dharmas (the view of a dharma-self): with ignorance and wrong views it covers over wisdom and understanding and obstructs the fruit of bodhi.

[The three vehicles] “Vehicle” means a conveyance; here it is a metaphor for the Dharma-gates that carry sentient beings across birth and death to the other shore of nirvāṇa. In accordance with the dull, middling, and keen faculties of sentient beings, the Buddha taught correspondingly the three teachings of the hearer vehicle, the solitary realizer vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle. The three vehicles are the small vehicle, the middle vehicle, and the great vehicle. The small vehicle is the hearer vehicle, the middle vehicle is the solitary realizer vehicle, and the great vehicle is the bodhisattva vehicle.

When attachment to self is wholly removed, one ends segmental birth and death and leaves the three realms; when attachment to dharmas is wholly removed, one ends transformation birth and death and realizes the Buddha-fruit.

[Because there is nothing to attain, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñā paramita, has no hindrance in the mind. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear, and, far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, he attains ultimate nirvāṇa.]

Because the ten thousand dharmas are all empty (illusory) and not one is attainable, the bodhisattva relies on the wondrous wisdom of prajñā to leave illusion, and so the mind has no hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear, and one is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions (within, not turning with thoughts; without, not pulled by objects), until one perfectly realizes the Buddha-fruit (ultimate nirvāṇa).

[Bodhisattva (bodhi-sattva)] Rendered in Chinese as “awakening being,” that is, a bodhisattva. [Far removed from inverted dreams and delusions] Here “dreams” refers to false thoughts, describing false thoughts as dreamlike, illusory, and unreal. Since everything is empty and unattainable, every stirring of the mind is inverted; hence “inverted” is used to describe false thoughts.

[Because there is nothing to attain, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñā paramita, has no hindrance in the mind] Since nothing is attained, nothing is lost. With neither gain nor loss, what hindrance could there be? The key is truly to awaken to this: nothing is attained. If the mind still has hindrances, then one is still entangled in fretting over gain and loss, and one must rely on prajñā paramita (the wondrous wisdom that leaves illusion) to do the work.
“Relying on prajñā paramita, therefore, the mind has no hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear, and, far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, one attains ultimate nirvāṇa.”

From this we see that whether one is awakened or deluded, whether one is a Buddha or a sentient being, all depends on the mind. This mind is the very mind of daily thought and deliberation; it can be good, and it can be evil; becoming a Buddha depends on it, being a human being depends on it, and falling into hell depends on it. The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says:
“This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the Buddhas’ correct and universal knowledge is born from the thought.”
The Mahayana Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground says:
“The Buddhas take the Dharma as the great teacher; the bodhi-path is realized through cultivation of the mind.”

[Correct and universal knowledge] That is, rightly and universally knowing—one of the Buddha’s ten honorific titles, meaning truly and universally knowing all dharmas. [Because there is nothing to attain] Where there is no gain, there is no loss. With neither gain nor loss, what hindrance is there? [Bodhisattva] The full Sanskrit name for a bodhisattva. [Relying on prajñā paramita, therefore the mind has no hindrance] Because all dharmas are illusory and unattainable, the bodhisattva practices relying on prajñā paramita (the practice of leaving illusion), and so the mind has no hindrance. “Prajñā paramita” is the practice of leaving illusion—not dwelling on marks while giving rise to the mind, and not being turned by objects. Master Guifeng says:
“Perceiving that all marks are empty, the mind is of itself without thought.”

[Inverted dreams and delusions] A diseased eye sees flowers in space and further summons fruit in space. [Far removed from inverted dreams and delusions] Within, not turning with thoughts; without, not pulled by objects. At the very beginning of the Diamond Sutra, the Buddha’s daily life is shown: “putting on his robe, taking up his bowl, begging for food, returning to his own place, eating the meal, putting away robe and bowl, washing his feet, spreading his seat, and sitting down.” Outwardly he is no different from the assembly. Yet the Buddha lives an awakened life: not grasping at marks, unmoved in suchness. Ordinary beings, by contrast, live a deluded life: the mind turns with objects, creating karma and receiving retribution. Hence it is called “inverted dreams and delusions.” The Sixth Patriarch says:

“When the preceding thought is deluded, one is an ordinary being; when the following thought is awakened, one is a Buddha. When the preceding thought clings to objects, that is affliction; when the following thought leaves objects, that is bodhi.”
[Ultimate nirvāṇa] Until one becomes a Buddha.

From kalpas without beginning, sentient beings have taken illusion as real and been caught in inverted dreams and delusions, and so they revolve in birth and death and suffer without cease. Now, knowing illusion, they at once leave it, and so the mind has no hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; no longer falsely taking a nightmare as real, they pass beyond all suffering and calamity, until they perfectly realize the Buddha-fruit.

No hindrance in the mind”—this is the actual realization of emptiness. The heart of upholding the Heart Sutra is to realize emptiness, to awaken to the truth that “all marks are false and vain,” and thereby to turn from the dust and merge with enlightenment, unstained and unattached, without reliance and without dwelling; only then is there true benefit. That demons arise from the mind is because one takes illusory marks as real. Once one has realized them to be false, the mind remains unmoved in suchness. As the saying goes: Meet a strange sight without strangeness, and the strangeness defeats itself. If one is truly thus, one can pass beyond all suffering and calamity, be far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, and attain ultimate nirvāṇa. The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says:
“Know it to be a flower in space, and there is no revolving.”
It also says:
“Knowing illusion, at once leaving it, without resort to expedient means; apart from illusion, at once awakened, with no graded sequence.”

[Emptiness] Another name for thusness. Thusness is the real nature free of the two attachments—attachment to self and attachment to dharmas. Wherever one cultivates the contemplation of emptiness and thereby frees oneself from these two attachments, the real nature of thusness vividly reveals itself; this real nature is called emptiness. [The two attachments] Attachment to self and attachment to dharmas. Attachment to self, also called attachment to the person-self, is the clinging to the idea that a person has a real, existing self. Attachment to dharmas, also called attachment to the dharma-self, is the clinging to the idea that all dharmas possess real substance and function.

[Turning away from the dust and merging with original enlightenment] “Dust” refers to the six sense-objects. “Turning away from the dust and merging with original enlightenment” means abandoning deluded clinging to the realm of sense-objects and uniting with original enlightenment. [Original enlightenment] All sentient beings have a self-nature that is pure; the essence of the mind is originally awake, apart from all delusive thought. For this reason it is called original enlightenment.
Q: How can one realize emptiness?
A: One must personally and closely see through amid the objects and conditions [of experience] until one reaches a state of no doubt. In the “Dream Wandering Collection
An Address to Attendant Qi on the Boat to Leiyang,” Master Hanshan says:
“The Buddha and the patriarchs taught people, in the midst of birth and death, to realize at once the patient acceptance of the unborn dharma
(“patient acceptance of the unborn dharma” means true wisdom abiding in the real principle of thusness, which is neither arising nor ceasing),

and they often wondered that people, within the unborn, should through delusion see arising and ceasing. This saying is like telling of dreams to a street crowd: those who hear it are not without clarity and boldness (the hearers are not unmoved or unkindled), only they have not yet realized the truth. In short, what is spoken is not what is heard, and what is heard is not what one sees. The ancients valued real realization precisely because they wished only to see through closely and personally amid the dharmas of birth and death—there is nothing else extraordinary about it. I have seen children who fear ghosts: walking at night, they would sense a thing following them and grow greatly frightened; though a loving mother kindly assures them that there is nothing at all, they still will not believe—it is only when they themselves come to conviction without doubt that they are at rest. Once one has reached that ground of no doubt, even if one were frightened by an actual ghost, one would simply laugh it off.

Formerly I traveled beyond the frontier. Riding through the night with a sturdy trooper, there was a stone by the roadside; the horse suddenly caught sight of it and started in fright, nearly throwing me to the ground. Thereupon I
(so I)

pulled in the reins and lashed it mightily, circling the stone dozens of times, then led it to gaze closely for a long while, and only after that let it run free; from then on the horse met nothing that startled it. Because of this I knew that a person traversing the perilous road of birth and death, testing the mind through every experience, must do exactly this before he is done.
(To urge the horse around the stone and make it gaze close, until it no longer doubted and no longer started, and only then stop.)
. Therefore the Avatamsaka uses Sudhana to set forth realization
(so the “Avatamsaka Sutra” uses the boy Sudhana’s fifty-three pilgrimages to make clear how one truly realizes)
; the hundred cities he passed through, the many good teachers he visited—even before a mountain of knives and a blaze of fire he drew back
(hesitant, wavering)
and only entered after being urged, and having entered he in fact attained the cool, great gate of liberation
(having truly realized that the mountain of knives and the blazing fire are but illusions).
Is this not what is meant by “urging the horse around the stone and making it gaze close”?
(Is it not precisely making him, by “urging the horse around the stone and making it gaze close,” see through it closely and personally?)
“From this we may observe that the Buddha and the patriarchs had no other excellence—they were simply able to gaze steadily upon the
(worldly)

marks. What the people of the world fear and dread—is it not birth, death, calamity, and harm? The Buddha and the patriarchs wished instead to lead people to realize the patient acceptance of the unborn within them, and moreover plainly said that within the unborn one delusively sees arising and ceasing.
(the Buddhas, amid the clear arising and ceasing, see only the unborn; sentient beings, amid the serene unborn, delusively see arising and ceasing.)
. Alas! What does this mean, after all? If it were not that
(if it were not that)
one gazes steadily until reaching the ground of no doubt, I fear that even though the Compassionate One kindly exhorted, [we] would
(probably)
also find it hard to escape fear and dread.
“Recently I
(in my recent days)
met with calamity for spreading the Dharma and provoked the sacred wrath
(Master Hanshan, for spreading the Dharma, was slandered; the emperor in wrath had him arrested and thrown into prison, and subjected him to harsh interrogation, with life and death uncertain)
; like a thunderbolt in broad daylight, at which those who hear stop their ears. From my arrest until my leaving
(exiled from the capital)

, more than two hundred days passed in which I endured hardships beyond telling. From first to last, as I watched, a single thought of joy never diminished from my usual days; all who saw it marveled as extraordinary. Yet birth, death, calamity, and harm—others were frightened on my account; and when they saw that my joy had not diminished, they were all the more astonished. I was not alarmed at what alarmed them, while they were alarmed at what did not alarm me—surely there is something of the Way in this! Attendant Qi, from a distance of three thousand li, came to my distress to question me in the dark prison. Then, by the grace of the sacred favor, I was exiled to Lingnan, and Qi accompanied me in the boat, whereupon I wrote this as a farewell. Alas! The perilous road of birth and death is just what one would fear; could it be that you have not heard of my joyful heart and take it for a dream? In days to come, verify me in the field of still extinction

((in days to come, when you realize the patient acceptance of the unborn (in the field of still extinction), you will verify that what I have said is a truthful statement. [Field of still extinction] The state of realizing the patient acceptance of the unborn—when delusion is exhausted and reality is revealed, stillness and extinction appear before you))
, and do not take today’s words as dream-talk.”
(For the annotations to the above instruction, see
Annotated Record of Master Hanshan’s Instruction: Closely Seeing Through
Q: What is the point of realizing emptiness?

A: Having realized emptiness, the mind no longer grasps at objects: within the world it crosses beyond suffering and calamity, and at the end of life it has done with birth and death. Master Hanshan was arrested and thrown into prison, tortured under harsh interrogation, with life and death uncertain, and all were afraid—yet the Master’s “single thought of joy never diminished from his usual days.” Why? Because he knew, and had realized, that this transient life is a dream, and so he was neither frightened nor alarmed.
Q: How does one apply the effort?
A: Awaken to the illusory and still the false. Master Guifeng says in his “Preface to the Collected Interpretations of the Source of Meditation”:

“When one awakens to the emptiness of all marks, the mind is of itself without thought. When a thought arises, awaken to it; having awakened, it is gone. The wondrous gateway of practice lies in this alone.”
Therefore prajñā paramita is the wondrous dharma that breaks illusion—let the sky-flowers whirl and tumble as they will, I remain calmly and utterly unmoved.

[When a thought arises, awaken] As soon as a delusive thought arises, one must at once wake up: this is an illusion! [Having awakened, it is gone] Once one has awakened, the mind is of itself without thought.

Q: The commonly circulated text of the “Heart Sutra” reads: “Because there is nothing to be attained, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñā paramita, dwells without hindrance in the mind. Because the mind is without hindrance, there is no fear; having gone beyond inverted dream-thoughts, [he attains] final nirvāṇa.” Why is it punctuated here as “Because there is nothing to be attained, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñā paramita, — therefore the mind is without hindrance. Because the mind is without hindrance, there is no fear; having gone beyond inverted dream-thoughts, [he attains] final nirvāṇa.”?

A: The “Heart Sutra” as translated by Master Xuanzang carries no punctuation at all. Punctuation marks were added by later people to make reading easier, according to the sense of the text. If it were punctuated as “Because there is nothing to be attained, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñā paramita, dwells without hindrance in the mind,” then the meaning would be: the bodhisattva, having nothing to attain, relies on prajñā paramita and so dwells without hindrance in the mind. Thus punctuated, the logic is not clear enough. The meaning of the sutra is: the bodhisattva, because he has nothing to attain, therefore relies on prajñā paramita; and because he relies on prajñā paramita, therefore his mind is without hindrance. Hence it is best punctuated as

“Because there is nothing to be attained, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñā paramita, — therefore the mind is without hindrance. Because the mind is without hindrance, there is no fear; having gone beyond inverted dream-thoughts, [he attains] final nirvāṇa.”
, which is fitting.
“The Buddhas of the three times, relying on prajñā paramita, attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”
The Buddhas of the three times, relying on prajñā paramita (the practice of leaving illusion), realized anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (attaining Buddhahood).
[Relying on prajñā paramita, therefore] The wondrous wisdom leaves illusion and is not turned by it. The “Diamond Sutra” says:
“One who is free of all marks is called a Buddha.”
[Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi] In Chinese: unsurpassed right and perfect enlightenment—attaining Buddhahood.
Q: How should one take up and uphold the “Heart Sutra”?
A: The sutra says:

“The bodhisattva, relying on prajñā paramita, — therefore the mind is without hindrance. Because the mind is without hindrance, there is no fear; having gone beyond inverted dream-thoughts, [he attains] final nirvāṇa.”

The key to upholding the “Heart Sutra” lies in “the mind is without hindrance.” Therefore one should examine at all times and everywhere: is the mind without hindrance? If the mind is hindered, that shows one is still clinging to certain illusions as real, and one must awaken from just this point. The “Nirvāṇa Sutra” says:
“All dharmas are false and illusory.”
The “Perfect Enlightenment Sutra” says:
“Seeing illusion, one immediately leaves it, without contrivance; leaving illusion, one is awake, with no gradations.”
One must ceaselessly realize, ceaselessly leave illusion, ceaselessly examine oneself. The “Diamond Sutra” says:
“One who is free of all marks is called a Buddha.”
“Therefore know that prajñā paramita is the great mantra, the great mantra of bright light, the supreme mantra, the unequalled mantra, able to remove all suffering. It is true, not false.”

From this it is known that prajñā paramita is the great-power dhāraṇī, the great-light dhāraṇī, the unsurpassed dhāraṇī, the dhāraṇī to which nothing is equal, able to remove all suffering—true, not false.

That which contains all without exception is called “great”; that which penetrates all without obstruction is called “spirit”; that to which nothing can be added is called “supreme”; that which has no peer is called “unequalled.”

[Unequalled] It describes the most honored, most precious, that to which nothing is equal. [Mantra] The Sanskrit dhāraṇī is rendered into Chinese as “zhòu,” a secret utterance that Buddhas and bodhisattvas set forth from samādhi. “Dhāraṇī” means to hold and uphold—embracing all dharmas and sustaining immeasurable meaning.
“Therefore the mantra of prajñā paramita is proclaimed. And the mantra is declared thus:”

Because prajñā paramita is the spirit-boat over the sea of suffering, the mantra of prajñā paramita is set forth so that beings may hold it in secret, to reap swift results and go straight to the other shore.
“Gate! Gate! Pāragate! Pārasaṃgate! Bodhi svāhā!”
Go! Go! Go to the other shore. Let everyone go to the other shore and swiftly realize the unsurpassed bodhi.

“Gate” means “go”; “pāra” means “to the other shore”—here “the other shore” refers to nirvāṇa; “saṃ” means “the multitude”; “bodhi” means “awakening”—here “bodhi” refers to the Buddha’s unsurpassed bodhi (unsurpassed right and perfect enlightenment); “svāhā” means “swift accomplishment.”

[Gate, gate] Paraphrase: go, go. [Pāragate] Paraphrase: go to the other shore. [Pārasaṃgate] Paraphrase: let everyone go to the other shore. [Bodhi svāhā] Paraphrase: swiftly realize the unsurpassed bodhi.

According to the meaning of this sutra—leaving illusion and emerging from the dream—here “go (gate)” means to leave illusion, and “go to the other shore (pāragate)” means to go to the far shore of nirvāṇa (to emerge from the dream of ignorance). The “Perfect Enlightenment Sutra” says:
“Seeing illusion, one immediately leaves it, without contrivance; leaving illusion, one is awake, with no gradations.”
The “Diamond Sutra” says:
“One who is free of all marks is called a Buddha.”
Therefore the mantra of prajñā paramita is freely translated as:
Leave illusion! Leave illusion!
Leave illusion and go to the other shore.
Let all leave illusion,
and swiftly realize nirvāṇa.
As for this mantra, Master Shengyi says in his “Heart Sutra Lecture Notes”:

“What is secret cannot be explained, nor is it known to others. In the Buddhist community many cultivate according to the exoteric teaching, and many also according to the esoteric—such as the Great Compassion Mantra, the Śūraṅgama Mantra, and the like—none of which can be explained. If they could be explained, they would not be called secret. The secret is like one drinking water, who knows for himself whether it is cold or warm; it cannot be spoken, cannot be explained, and is known only to oneself. Today, however, I will roughly set out the meaning of this mantra: Gate, gate—go, go. Pāragate—go to the other shore. Pārasaṃgate—the multitude goes to the other shore. Bodhi svāhā—swiftly accomplish and realize bodhi.”

blocks.text: Chapter on the Study of Illusion

inline.s: (Excerpted from the “Great Prajñā Paramita Sutra
Chapter Eleven on the Study of Illusion”)

[Note] This passage in the “Great Prajñā Paramita Sutra” is close in content to the “Heart Sutra”; setting the two side by side, one can understand the meaning of the “Heart Sutra” all the more deeply.
At that time, the wisdom-life Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, if someone were to ask, “When an illusory person studies prajñā paramita, will he attain sarvajña
(“Sarvajña” is rendered into Chinese as “knowledge of all modes,” that is, the great wisdom of the Buddha’s ultimate and perfect fruition)
or not
(read as “fǒu,” meaning “or not”)
? When an illusory person studies dhyāna paramita
(the paramita of meditative concentration)
, vīrya paramita
(the paramita of vigor)
, kṣānti paramita
(the paramita of patience)
, śīla paramita
(the paramita of precepts)
, dāna paramita
(the paramita of giving)
, studies the four foundations of mindfulness

(namely the mindfulness of body, of feeling, of mind, and of dharmas. Mindfulness of body is contemplating that the body is impure; mindfulness of feeling is contemplating that feeling is suffering; mindfulness of mind is contemplating that the mind is impermanent; mindfulness of dharmas is contemplating that dharmas are without a self)
, and even the eighteen exclusive dharmas
(the eighteen dharmas of excellences belonging only to the Buddha; because they are restricted to the Buddha and are not shared with the three vehicles, they are called “exclusive”)
, and the knowledge of all modes
(the knowledge of all modes is the Buddha’s wisdom that penetrates the general and particular marks of all dharmas, guiding beings and severing delusion)
—will he attain sarvajña or not?” What am I to answer?

The Buddha told Subhuti: I will ask you in turn; answer me as you see fit. Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from illusion? Are feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness different from illusion? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said: What do you think? Is the eye different from illusion? And so on up to: is the mind different from illusion
(this asks whether the six sense-organs differ from illusion)
? Are forms, up to dharmas, different from illusion
(this asks whether the six sense-objects differ from illusion)
? Is the eye-element, up to the mind-consciousness element, different from illusion
(this asks whether the eighteen elements differ from illusion)
? Is eye-contact, up to mind-contact—the feeling arising from the conditions of eye-contact, up to the feeling arising from the conditions of mind-contact

(when the eye meets forms that are agreeable or disagreeable, feeling of pleasure or pain arises—this is called “feeling born of eye-contact”; this asks the contact-feelings produced when the six sense-organs meet the six sense-objects)
, different from illusion? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One.
What do you think? Are the four foundations of mindfulness different from illusion? And on up to the eightfold noble path
(namely the eight right paths, the eight paths of the sages; cultivating these eight right paths one can realize the fruit of arhatship)
—is it different from illusion? No, World-Honored One.
What do you think? Are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness different from illusion? No, World-Honored One.
Subhuti, what do you think? Is dāna paramita different from illusion? And on up to the eighteen exclusive dharmas—are they different from illusion? No, World-Honored One.

Subhuti, what do you think? Is anuttara-samyak-sambodhi different from illusion? No, World-Honored One. Why? Form is not different from illusion; illusion is not different from form; form is illusion, illusion is form. World-Honored One, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness are not different from illusion; illusion is not different from feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness; consciousness is illusion, illusion is consciousness. World-Honored One, the eye is not different from illusion; illusion is not different from the eye; the eye is illusion, illusion is the eye; the feeling born of the conditions of eye-contact, up to the feeling born of the conditions of mind-contact, is likewise. World-Honored One, the four foundations of mindfulness are not different from illusion; illusion is not different from the four foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness are illusion, illusion is the four foundations of mindfulness; and on up to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi not being different from illusion, illusion not being different from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is illusion, illusion is anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? Does illusion have defilement and purity? No, World-Honored One. Subhuti, what do you think? Does illusion have arising and ceasing? No, World-Honored One.
